title: Counting by order in a cyclic group
promptMarkdown:
Let $G=\langle a\rangle$ be a cyclic group of order $n$.

1. Prove that for every positive divisor $d$ of $n$ the group $G$ has exactly one subgroup of order $d$, namely $\langle a^{n/d}\rangle$, and that $G$ has no subgroups of any other order.
2. Prove that for every positive divisor $d$ of $n$ the number of elements of $G$ of order exactly $d$ is $\varphi(d)$, where $\varphi$ is Euler's function.
3. Deduce the identity $\displaystyle\sum_{d\mid n}\varphi(d)=n$.
4. For $\mathbb Z_{36}$, tabulate the number of elements of each possible order and check the identity numerically.
hintLadder: Every subgroup of a cyclic group is cyclic: $H=\langle a^m\rangle$ with $m$ the least positive exponent occurring in $H$. Why must $m$ divide $n$, and what is $|H|$ in terms of $m$?
Use the order formula $|a^k|=n/\gcd(k,n)$ to identify the order of $\langle a^{n/d}\rangle$.
An element of order $d$ generates a subgroup of order $d$; by part 1 there is only one. How many generators does a cyclic group of order $d$ have (Corollary 4.1.14)?
Every element of $G$ has exactly one order, and that order divides $n$. Count $G$ by sorting its elements according to their orders.

deterministicChecks.description: Euler's function φ(d) is used for the count of elements of order d
tables for particular n are not a proof for all n

criteria.criterion: Every subgroup is ⟨a^m⟩ with m | n and order n/m, so subgroup orders divide n and for each divisor d the only subgroup of order d is ⟨a^{n/d}⟩ (whose order is confirmed by the order formula).

levels.description: Existence, uniqueness and the exclusion of other orders all argued.

levels.label: partially met
levels.description: Existence via the order formula, uniqueness or the divisibility m | n not argued.

criteria.criterion: Elements of order d are exactly the generators of the unique subgroup of order d, which is cyclic of order d and has φ(d) generators.

levels.label: met

levels.label: partially met

criteria.criterion: Partition of G by order of elements gives n = Σ_{d|n} φ(d).

checkExamples.label: general argument
checkExamples.text: Each element of order $d$ generates the unique subgroup of order $d$, which is cyclic of order $d$ and so has $\varphi(d)$ generators; hence there are exactly $\varphi(d)$ elements of order $d$ for every divisor $d$ of $n$, and summing over all divisors counts every element of $G$ once.

checkExamples.label: no Euler function
checkExamples.text: There are exactly d elements of order d, since the subgroup of order d has d elements.

checkExamples.label: tables only
checkExamples.text: For n=6 there are 1, 1, 2, 2 elements of orders 1, 2, 3, 6; for n=4 there are 1, 1, 2 of orders 1, 2, 4; for n=8 the table is 1, 1, 2, 4. So the claim holds.
